data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Extinction events kill organisms, whereas network nodes can be rebooted or restored from backup.","Biological evolution is slow and non-directed; network architecture can be rapidly redesigned to mitigate known tail risks.","The 'tail' for networks may include recoverable failures, whereas extinction is permanent."],"overturn_conditions":["Evidence that decentralized networks can survive certain classes of global shocks (e.g., by being offline or air-gapped) that would destroy a large service.","Proof that the 'tail' is not actually reachable within the operational lifespan of the system."],"shared_structure":["Both systems are subject to external environmental shocks.","In the limit, these shocks are large enough to overwhelm internal defenses.","The probability of such shocks is non-zero and accumulates over time."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_002"],"transfer_claims":["Both large and decentralized networks share a common, unavoidable vulnerability to extreme shared causes.","Arguments for the superior resilience of either topology that ignore tail risks are incomplete."]},"claim":"Extreme value statistics imply that catastrophic shared causes will eventually dominate any topology, meaning both large and decentralized systems are equally doomed to correlated failure at the tails; decentralization only delays the inevitable.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the timeframe is finite and short enough that tail events are negligible.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the large service can physically isolate itself from global shocks (e.g., offline redundancy).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If decentralized nodes are geographically and logically diverse enough to survive some global shocks that would kill a centralized service.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"In the limit of infinite time, the probability of a catastrophic shared cause (e.g., a massive solar flare, a global internet backbone failure, or a critical protocol bug) approaches 1. Since such events affect all nodes regardless of topology, they introduce perfect correlation in failure at the extreme tails. The large service's internal redundancy is useless against these global shocks, and the decentralized network's independence is illusory under such shocks.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
